attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click on each asset to notice their names and what type of asset they are?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What images, tiles, and tilemaps do you notice in My Assets?

❓ What might each asset be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja notices the names of each of the assets on the left side of the screen, prompt them to consider how the asset might be used in the project, based on its name. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to click on each tilemap to notice how they are different and similar. Encourage the ninja to notice how the different tile assets are used in the tilemap and which tiles have their walls turned on.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the assets in My Assets. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images, tiles, and tilemaps in My Assets. Click on each asset to view its name, then think about what it might be used for in this project. Click on the 2 different tilemaps, notice the layout, where each tile is used and which tiles have their walls turned on.

steps.hints: ❓Did you fill in the empty space with the different background tile assets, leaving the path tiles as is?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might the moonTilemap asset be used in this project?

❓ What tile assets might you use to fill in the empty space in the moonTilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they should add assets to the tiles that already have their walls turned on. The ninja should not change the path tiles at all, as these will be necessary when the tilemaps switch throughout the project.
steps.instructions:
Design an alternate tilemap with the same path tiles. 


Open the moonTilemap asset in My Assets, and notice that the path tiles are the same as the cactusTilemap, but there are no background tiles. 


Use the background tile assets (not the path tiles) from My Tiles to fill in the empty space on the moonTilemap asset so that it looks different from the cactusTilemap asset. Since the sprite will alternate between the two “worlds”, do not change the path tiles in either tilemap.


Click Done to update the moonTilemap asset in My Assets.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use // to add comments to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming assets, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments.
steps.instructions:
Add code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add comments for directions, project set up, sprite set up, and tilemap overlap events.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, and the asset type, followed by the name of the asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap asset be typed in the setCurrentTilemap function?

❓ What background color might match the theme of the cactusTilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding a background color to the project.
steps.instructions:
Set a background color and tilemap to appear on screen!


Display a  background color under // project set up. 


Open Scene and drag [set tilemap to (tilemap)] underneath. To access the tilemap created in My Assets, type assets and a dot operator before tilemap`` inside the parentheses of the setCurrentTilemap function. Then type cactusTilemap inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Click ▶ to see the cactusTilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the documentation for help with creating a Player sprite, setting its scale, and moving the sprite around the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where can you find the coordinates of a specific tile in the tilemap editor?

❓ Why might the scale of the Player sprite need to be decreased?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Explain that coordinates begin at 0 and increase from left to right (column) and top to bottom (row). The ninja can use their cursor to hover over a specific tile, then find its coordinates in the bottom left corner of the tilemap editor.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding a sprite and/or changing its scale.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project.


Add code to create a sprite in the project underneath // sprite set up. 


Replace img`...` by typing assets, a dot operator, and image. Type the name given to the sprite’s image asset surrounded by 2 backticks ` `.  


Set the Player sprite’s scale to .7, so that the Player sprite appears smaller and moves around the tilemap more easily. 


Open Scene and drag [place mySprite on top of (loc)] underneath the Player sprite’s code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. Update the tilemap coordinates in the location parameter to place the Player sprite in the top left corner of the tilemap. Then, add code to move the Player sprite around the tilemap with direction buttons.


Click ▶ then test the Player sprite’s code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the tile parameter in the onOverlapTile events with the names of  the moon and cactus tile assets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is setting a tilemap overlap event in the JavaScript editor similar and different than the blocks editor?

❓ What code should be used to set the moon and cactus tile assets as each tile argument?

❓ How can you check the name of a tile stored in My Assets?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that in the blocks editor, tilemap overlap events appeared as container blocks, whereas in the JavaScript editor, they appear as block statements with their own pair of curly brackets { }. In the blocks editor, the ninja was able to use a code completion tool to select the tile parameter. In the JavaScript editor, code must be used (directly as an image or an asset) to specify the tile argument.

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``. 

💡 If the ninja forgot the name of the tile assets, they should go to My Assets, then select each tile to see the preview with the asset name on the left side.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps a specific tile!


Open Scene and drag 2 [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (tile) at (location)] underneath // tilemap overlap events. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 


scene.onOverlapTile(SpriteKind.Player, img` `, function(sprite: Sprite, location: tiles.Location) {...})

The onOverlapTile function takes 3 parameters: kind, tile, handler. Keep the kind parameter set to Player. Set the tile parameter in the first onOverlapTile event to the moon tile saved in My Assets. Replace img` `, with assets followed by a dot operator. Use tile as the asset type, then type the name given to the moon tile inside the 2 backticks ``.  


Set the tile parameter in the second onOverlapTile event to the cactus tile asset.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the tilemap asset names in the setCurrentTilemap functions so that the tilemap changes correctly on overlap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap be typed in each setCurrentTilemap function?

❓ What background color might match the theme of the moonTilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``. 

💡 If the ninja forgot the name of the tilemap assets, they should go to My Assets, then select each tilemap to see the preview with the asset name on the left side.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding a background color to the project.
steps.instructions:
Switch the tilemaps and background color when the Player sprite overlaps the moon or cactus tiles! 


Open Scene and drag [set tilemap to (tilemap)] inside both onOverlapTile events. Replace tilemap`` with the moonTilemap asset in setCurrentTilemap in the first onOverlapTile event and the cactusTilemap asset in the second onOverlapTile event.


Add code to change the background color inside both onOverlapTile events. Change the background to a different color when the moonTilemap asset is displayed, then change the background back to the original color when the cactusTilemap asset is displayed. 


Click ▶ to test the tile overlap code to see the tilemap and background color switch.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the documentation for help setting a dialog frame and box?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code should be used to set the frame image asset as the image parameter in the setDialogFrame function?

❓ What information might be shared with the user at the beginning of the project?  


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``.
steps.instructions:
Add directions at the beginning of the project. 


Add code to set a dialog frame under // directions. Replace img` `, with assets followed by a dot operator. Use image as the asset type, then type the name given to the frame image inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Then, add code to add text to and set the position of the dialog box.


Click ▶ to see the directions appear on the screen

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the marquee tool to select the 16 x 16 image, then drag one of the corner white boxes to resize the image so that it is 32 x 32 pixels?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How can an asset be duplicated?

❓ What tool is needed to change the size of an asset in the editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Once the ninja has opened My Assets, prompt them to select the Player sprite’s image asset. On the left side of the screen, a “duplicate” button will appear. Once the asset has been duplicated, remind the ninja to rename the asset on the bottom right of the editor.

💡 Help the ninja use the marquee tool to resize the duplicated Player sprite’s image. Remind them to make sure the image fills the entire space, making sure that the length and width of the image are scaled evenly.

💡 Point out to the ninja that changing the cursor image is a fun way to customize a project. This can be done by using the Player sprite’s image, or another important asset to give the user a sneak peek into the project.
steps.instructions:
Update the cursor image that appears on the dialog box.


Click the Assets menu, select the Player sprite image, then click Duplicate. Click edit to open the second image, and rename the asset cursorImage. 

Resize the canvas to 32 x 32 on the bottom left corner. Use the marquee tool  to select the entire sprite image. Click and drag one of the corner white boxes to resize the image to fill the entire canvas. Click Done to update the asset.


Open Game, drag [set dialog cursor to (cursor)] before showLongText. Replace img` ` with assets followed by a dot operator. Use image as the asset type, then type the name given to the cursor image inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear as a large cursor image on the screen.

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that switches the tilemap when a sprite overlaps a certain tile.

validationItems.text: Display a tilemap asset on screen.
Create 1 sprite using an image asset and place it on a specific tile coordinate.
Change the tilemaps and background colors when the Player sprite overlaps specific tiles
Use an image asset as a dialog frame.
Create a cursor image asset and use it in a dialog box.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about tilemap overlap events and how to make different things happen when sprites overlap different tiles and walls. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: The Big Event
badges.description: Use events to control what happens to sprites navigating a tilemap in a project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Touch Controls
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite overlaps a specific tile.

badges.title: A Chain of Reactions
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite hits a wall.

badges.title: A Glyph in the System
badges.description: Use an image asset as a cursor image in a dialog box.

badges.title: Save for Later
badges.description: Create an array to store all of the locations of a specific tile type on a tilemap.

badges.title: Invisible Walls
badges.description: Turn a wall on or off at a specific location on a tilemap.
